latest_articles.title: Communal coping and psychological well-being among graduate students: A test of the extended theoretical model of communal coping
latest_articles.abstract: This study tested the extended theoretical model of communal coping in a sample of 554 graduate students, examining both predictors and outcomes of communal coping. Communal coping occurs when individuals perceive stressors as shared and take collective action to manage them, thereby acting as a potential resource for graduate students. Results from an online survey demonstrated that graduate students’ academic stress was associated negatively with psychological well-being. Counter to our hypotheses, relational closeness did not moderate the relationship between academic stress and either communal coping dimension (shared appraisal or joint action). However, subsequent post hoc regression models suggested that shared appraisal was predicted by both academic stress and relational closeness, whereas joint action was predicted by relational closeness but not academic stress. A conditional process model positing that communal coping indirectly impacts psychological well-being through coping efficacy (contingent on openness to communicate about academic stressors and communication efficacy) was not supported. Alternative model testing revealed that although communal coping did not indirectly impact well-being through coping efficacy, joint action directly impacted psychological well-being above and beyond coping efficacy. Theoretical and practical implications for how graduate students cope with academic stress are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Who is Persuaded by Stories to Help Combat Period Poverty? Gender Difference in Processing and Responding to Individual and Collective Narratives
latest_articles.abstract: Period poverty (a lack of access to menstrual products, sanitation, and education), affects over a billion people worldwide, posing threats to physical, mental, and emotional well-being. Effective messaging is critical to combating this public health issue. This study investigated how message format (narrative versus non-narrative) and narrative focus (individual versus collective narrative) shape audience members’ processing of and responses to Period poverty messaging. In a between-subjects online experiment withU.S. adults (N = 1104), participants were randomly assigned to one of three message conditions. Results revealed no significant effects of message format or narrative focus in the full sample. However, subgroup estimates revealed significant indirect effects. Within the male subsample, the individual narrative (vs. non-narrative) increased policy support and donation intention through transportation and anger. Additionally, the individual (vs. collective) narrative enhanced policy support via compassion and anger. Within the female subsample, persuasive outcomes were not shaped by message format or narrative focus. Overall, these patterns suggest that audience gender identity may warrant further investigation as a potential boundary condition in communicating period poverty. The results highlight the importance of tailoring period poverty messages to audiences with different genders and advancing theory on identity-contingent narrative persuasion.

latest_articles.title: Effortful Control and Media Use from Birth to Age 5: A Meta-Analysis
latest_articles.abstract: Effortful control—the ability to regulate attention, emotion, and behavior—is essential for adaptive functioning. It develops rapidly during the first five years of life, a period when media exposure is evolving. However, inconsistent findings across studies have left this relation unclear. This meta-analysis examined the relation between effortful control and media use during early childhood (birth to age 5). Data were synthesized from 26 studies, comprising 246 effect sizes and 19,971 children across 20 countries, five of which were represented by multiple studies (United States, Canada, China, Finland, and Türkiye). We investigated the overall association between effortful control and media use and the role of potential moderators. Results showed that the overall association was significant, indicating that children with higher effortful control engaged in lower levels of media use, and this relation became stronger with age. Media interactivity moderated the association, such that noninteractive and uncategorized media use were more negatively associated with effortful control than interactive media, controlling for age, media quantity, measurement types, and study design. These findings identify effortful control as a temperament-based individual difference associated with early media use and underscore the importance of developmental timing and media interactivity in moderating this relation.

latest_articles.title: Reconceptualizing Advertising Measurement in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
latest_articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling large-scale creative automation, dynamic personalization, and AI-mediated consumer decision journeys. Existing measurement systems were developed for human-authored and relatively stable communication environments and do not capture how GenAI systems cocreate brand touchpoints with advertisers or mediate consumer evaluations of brands. In this study, we develop an integrated triadic framework for understanding the GenAI-mediated advertising landscape and reconceptualizes the action–mindset–behavior–finance measurement architecture to reflect an advertising process that is increasingly recursive, nonlinear, and adaptive. In doing so, we distinguish between traditional metrics that remain relevant but require reconceptualization and novel metrics unique to GenAI-assisted advertising systems. In addition, we extend the framework beyond firm-centered outcomes to incorporate stakeholder-oriented metrics relevant to employees, regulators, investors, and society. The framework offers guidance for scholars and managers seeking to evaluate GenAI advertising while maintaining transparency, trust, and competitive integrity. The study concludes with a future research agenda and crosscutting priorities addressing measurement, governance, accountability, and methodological challenges associated with GenAI-assisted advertising.
affiliations: Boston University Questrom School of Business

latest_articles.title: Perceiving the News as Toxic: A Longitudinal, Cross-National Analysis of Negative News Evaluations in Flanders and Ireland
latest_articles.abstract: In today’s media environment, where information overload, negativity, and news fatigue are increasingly common, news can feel toxic. Yet little research examines how users perceive this toxicity and adjust their news practices in response. This study addresses that gap through a repeated cross-sectional analysis of Flanders and Ireland. Drawing on DNR-data from 2017-2025 and latent class analysis, we identify three archetypal news repertoires: Panoramic, Limited, and Traditional. Our findings reveal a shift toward limited repertoires, particularly among younger and less socioeconomically advantaged groups, while panoramic repertoires have become rarer, and traditional repertoires have remained stable. These shifts are associated with negative news attitudes, including distrust, avoidance, disinterest, fake news concerns and perceived fake news exposure. The cross-national comparison highlights sharper transitions in Flanders, whereas Irish users retained higher engagement, though early disengagement emerged. By linking negative attitudes or evaluations with changes in repertoires, we contribute to audience research and underscore the need to reconsider the journalism-audience relationship as disengagement is no longer marginal but increasingly mainstream. From a user perspective, repertoire narrowing may be understood as a coping response, although it risks deepening informational inequalities.

latest_articles.title: Advertising with HAART: Introducing Human–AI Asymmetric Relationship Theory
latest_articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)is rapidly reconfiguring advertising from message delivery and optimization to relationship-like exchanges between consumers and brands. While existing work has explained these interactions through social response accounts and interpersonal relationship theories, this lens risks overlooking a defining structural mismatch: AI agents convincingly enact relational characteristics but cannot experience relational benefits, costs, or commitment. Perceived mutuality can be high even when the underlying relational capacity for reciprocity is absent. We introduce human–AI asymmetric relationship theory (HAART), which conceptualizes AI-mediated relationships as relationally expressive yet structurally one-sided. HAART advances three tenets: (1) inherent AI agent characteristics limit relational reciprocity; (2) AI agents mask these limits through performative relationship actions, defined as linguistic, paralinguistic, and interactional behaviors that simulate relational engagement; and (3) when this masking succeeds, an asymmetric relationship emerges, characterized by asymmetries in dependence, risk, and control. We develop six propositions that detail the positive (e.g., enhanced support) and negative (e.g., heightened vulnerability) consequences for consumers and brands, and provide implications for theory, practice, and policy.

latest_articles.title: Expanded documentary and immersive technologies: Ludic logics and heritage mediation in ARTE’s interactive experiences
latest_articles.abstract: This article examines the transformation of contemporary documentary practices through immersive and interactive technologies, including virtual reality, augmented reality and game-based narrative structures. Positioned within debates on media convergence, the study argues that expanded documentary forms do not merely hybridise non-fiction with entertainment but reconfigure documentary epistemology through embodied immersion, procedural authorship and guided participation. Drawing on theories of expanded cinema, interactive documentary and game studies, the article clarifies the concept of ludic logics and distinguishes it from gamification and serious games. A qualitative comparative analysis of emblematic immersive documentary projects is conducted using a shared analytical grid focused on immersion, agency, narrative organisation and ethical positioning. The findings show that immersive non-fiction fosters situated and affective forms of knowledge while introducing new tensions between agency and authorial control. The article contributes to documentary and media convergence studies by providing a conceptually precise and methodologically replicable framework for analysing immersive non-fiction.

latest_articles.title: The fallacy of AI-generated podcasts: the case of Google NotebookLM
latest_articles.abstract: This paper critically examines science communication discourse produced through AI-generated podcasts, created via Google NotebookLM. We propose a rhetorical-argumentative framework to verify whether podcasts mediating scientific reports propagate quality discourse or mis−/dis-information. We apply this framework to the qualitative analysis of a corpus of podcasts stemming from scientific reports about communication and media research. The study reveals that podcasts produced via the ‘Audio Overview’ feature of Google NotebookLM, though engaging, trivialize content, propagate biases, and draw unwarranted inferences that misrepresent authors' intentions. The integration of dialectical and rhetorical components within our discourse analysis surfaced the presence of fallacies and misleading ways of packaging and presenting information. This misrepresentation risks undermining research integrity, as authors are not guaranteed the opportunity to verify the accuracy of their work before dissemination, and it spreads misinformation, instead of ensuring quality science communication to inform policymaking.

latest_articles.title: “‘Oh, women always…’. Yeah Image 1.” The mediated construction of medical gaslighting in an Instagram echo chamber
latest_articles.abstract: The use of the term gaslighting has increased prominently over the last few decades, both as a lay notion and a scholarly framework in the social sciences. Medical gaslighting, however, remains under researched, especially within digitally mediated discourse analysis. This paper addresses this gap by examining the construction of medical gaslighting as mediated discourse, that is, by considering how platform affordances and algorithms alongside user participation shape understandings of medical gaslighting. The study thus responds to calls to investigate how users react to perceived gaslighting on social media as well as how the possible formation of a “good echo chamber” may provide sources of epistemic contestation ( Pohlhaus, 2020 ; Shane et al., 2022 ). To carry out this research, a topical corpus on medical gaslighting was compiled and analysed. The corpus consisted of a National Public Radio post from Instagram, relevant metadata and user-generated comments. The analysis drew insights from mediated discourse analysis, media studies, pragmatics and identity frameworks. The post was qualitatively analysed and a corpus-assisted discourse analysis approach was adopted to examine user-generated comments. Findings reveal how Instagram's algorithms and affordances, together with discourse dynamics mediate the construction of medical gaslighting, which emerged as a socially recognized practice. Further, a largely supportive “good echo chamber” was generated in which strong agreement, epistemic validation and collaboration outweighed dissent, allowing users to contest medical dismissal and repair damaged epistemic identities.

latest_articles.title: An analysis of the role of gender in news assignment processes of media organizations in Türkiye
latest_articles.abstract: This study explores how women journalists in Türkiye perceive and experience gendered assignment patterns, professional inequalities, and structural barriers within media organizations. Drawing on semi-structured qualitative interviews with 20 female journalists working in newspapers, television channels, news agencies, and news websites in Türkiye, it investigates how women make sense of the assignment practices they encounter and what implications these practices carry for their career development and professional recognition. The findings show that participants experience gender-based inequalities in opportunities and career progression as being shaped by structural hierarchies that limit access to politically and economically significant news beats and require greater effort to achieve professional recognition.

latest_articles.title: “Your voice says a lot about you”: engendering masculinities in incel communities through voice
latest_articles.abstract: In September 2023, the X account for the Vers and Lukas podcast posted a link to the “Voicecel Test.” Using a term from the incel community, a portmanteau of “voice” and “incel,” this tool promises to help users discover how their voices are perceived—whether they project the “squeaky unaesthetic high voice” of an incel or the attractive tones of a “deep voice Chad.” The post went viral, garnering 2 million views in two days. This paper takes the Voicecel Test as an entry point to examine the voicecel phenomenon in incel culture to show how, in our audio-driven digital landscape, the voice gains saliency in making the gendered self legible. Through an interface analysis of the Voicecel Test site, as well as a feminist critical discourse analysis of digital incel spaces, we examine how participants in these communities (re)construct gendered voices, and how these constructions demonstrate Mickey Vallee’s conceptualization of the voice as an “imaginary organ” through which subjects perform gender. We argue that discourses surrounding the voicecel are critical to their engendering of normative masculinities, and for the way they bring these supposedly fringe frameworks closer to the mainstream.

latest_articles.title: Configurational Pathways to Reader Engagement with Online Weight Management Promotion in China: A Crisp-Set Qualitative Comparative Analysis
latest_articles.abstract: Abnormal body weight has become an increasingly prominent public health concern in China. In response, national health authorities launched a three-year Weight Management Year campaign, disseminating extensive online risk communication to promote public awareness and healthier lifestyles. Despite these efforts, reader engagement (RE) varies substantially, raising questions about how health risk can be communicated more effective. Previous studies have explored various antecedents of RE, but often in isolation, making it difficult to capture the complex interplay of factors in real-world settings. Grounded in the heuristic-systematic model, this study applies crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis to examine conjunctural causation among three systematic and two heuristic cues in shaping RE across 61 WeChat articles issued by health authorities and hospitals. The analysis identifies four pathways leading to strong engagement and six pathways resulting in weak engagement. Strong RE appears to emerges through systematic-dominant, heuristic-compensatory, and dual-cue reinforcing configurations, whereas weak RE reflect mismatches between message features and audience expectations or limited heuristic support. Overall, the findings reveal causal asymmetry and multiple conjunctural causation in RE, highlighting the complexity of online health communication and the need for context-sensitive communication strategies.
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business

latest_articles.title: From constituencies to audiences: lessons from Brazil about audience analytics in representative politics
latest_articles.abstract: The pursuit of audiences is a key driver of the mediatization of politics, yet it remains unclear how parliamentarians carry out this task. Drawing on interviews with members of Brazil’s Congress, this study investigates how politicians incorporate audience analytics into their communication strategies. It introduces a conceptual framework of audience perception – distinguishing among loyalists, followers, and audience reservoirs – to explain how politicians interpret digital publics. Findings reveal that parliamentarians’ perceptions of their audiences differ from their perceptions of electoral bases. Their follower base undergoes context collapse, disembedding audiences from their social context. Digital media re-embed these constituencies in platform contexts, wherein parliamentarians believe they must become always-on content producers, perform authenticity, and engage in information cycles. These findings reveal that audience analytics incentivize a sales orientation in parliamentary communication, distorting representation by recasting audiences as targets of influence rather than publics to whom politicians are accountable.

latest_articles.title: Skewed toward uniformity? Investigating algorithmic stereotyping and amplification in AI-generated images
latest_articles.abstract: As text-to-image generative artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly shapes visual communication, concerns are growing about its role in reproducing social stereotypes. While recent algorithm auditing studies have advanced our understanding of stereotypical AI-generated imagery, they have largely focused on a narrow set of stereotypes – primarily gender and race – overlooking more nuanced forms. Addressing this gap, our study adopts a case-sensitive approach that conceptualizes stereotypes as multi-layered phenomena composed of multiple, context-specific indicators. Applying the Draw-a-Scientist Test framework, we analyzed stereotypical representations of scientists in images generated by DALL·E 3 and examined potential amplification by benchmarking against Google Images. Specifically, we compared 16 stereotype indicators across six stereotype subjects. Using Latent Class Analysis, we identified six classes reflecting distinct patterns of stereotypical depiction. Our findings show that DALL·E not only produces highly stereotypical portrayals of scientists but also amplifies these patterns compared to Google Images. Both image sources lack adequate visual references for disciplines beyond the traditional laboratory context – a pattern we interpret as epistemic narrowing, whereby diverse forms of knowledge production are reduced to a uniform, laboratory-based representation of science. We conclude by discussing potential drivers of epistemic narrowing, the broader implications of algorithmic visibility, and mitigation strategies.

latest_articles.title: Inoculating against fatalistic beliefs: a comparative test of narrative and non-narrative strategies
latest_articles.abstract: This study compares the effectiveness of narrative and non-narrative inoculation messages in reducing fatalistic beliefs and fostering resistance to conflicting cancer information. A two-phase randomized experiment (N = 572 in Phase 1; n = 332 in Phase 2) tested their effects on counterarguing against attack, cancer fatalism, perceived efficacy, and intentions to adopt cancer risk-reduction behaviors. Compared with control, both inoculation messages reduced cancer fatalism, enhanced perceived efficacy, and increased certain intentions to adopt certain risk-reduction behaviors. Narrative inoculation elicited more counterarguing against attack than the non-narrative counterpart. Inoculation effects also varied by baseline fatalism, functioning therapeutically by immediately reducing initially high fatalism and, more modestly, prophylactically by maintaining initially low fatalism. These findings extend inoculation theory by elucidating the role of message format in sustaining resistance to negative media effects, and by demonstrating the theory’s potential dual prophylactic–therapeutic functionality in a fatalistic belief context.
affiliations: Wee Kim Wee School of Communication and Information, Nanyang Technological University ,

latest_articles.title: Translanguaging Practices Inside and Outside the Home: Children of Kabyle Immigrants in the UK
latest_articles.abstract: This paper explores the language practices of Kabyle immigrant families. Drawing on language ideology and translanguaging, this paper examines how these families and their children communicate and bring distinct histories, narratives, and trajectories to interaction both offline and online, complemented by diverse linguistic and semiotic resources. The analysis allows for an understanding of how “being Kabyle” for parents and their children has involved both the ability of speaking and learning their heritage language, while highlighting the role of migration trajectories and multicultural environments in shaping the individuals’ perceptions and fostering their acceptance of cultural and linguistic diversity.

latest_articles.title: Press freedom in a post-authoritarian context: evolving challenges for Bangladeshi journalists after Sheikh Hasina
latest_articles.abstract: Authoritarian constraints on press freedom manifest across diverse political contexts, from typical illiberal democracies to flawed democracies. While substantial scholarship examines journalistic challenges under authoritarian rule, the dynamics of press freedom in recent post-authoritarian transitions remain underexplored. Drawing on in-depth interviews with journalists from Bangladesh, this article investigates how press freedom evolves in these settings. Findings show that an authoritarian regime change does not guarantee press freedom or journalist safety. The study makes three theoretical contributions. First, ownership structures and political pressures from authoritarian periods persist after regime transitions. Second, control over the press may shift from predictable, top-down tools (laws and state agencies) to more scattered, bottom-up forces, such as street intimidation and social media harassment. Finally, the press-power relationship is often renegotiated rather than automatically liberalized following authoritarian collapse.
affiliations: Colorado State University, Fort Collins, Colorado, USA
University of Minnesota Twin Cities, Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA
University of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri, USA

latest_articles.title: Algorithmic News Selection Under News Avoidance: Assessing News Values on Chinese Tiktok (Douyin)
latest_articles.abstract: This study explores how recommendation algorithms on Douyin respond to users’ growing disengagement from news by shaping the visibility of news content. Adopting an agent-based testing (ABT) approach, we conducted a 2 (intentional news avoidance: 0% vs. 100%) × 2 (unintentional news avoidance: 50% vs. 100%) between-subject experiment to simulate distinct user behaviors and capture large-scale data from news-related videos. Findings indicated that two avoidance behavioral patterns result in contrasting algorithmic outcomes which reinforce or weaken certain news values such as prominence, uniqueness, timeliness, and influence. A significant interaction effect further reveals that the influence of intentional news avoidance on the news values of influence diminishes as users’ preference for non-news content increases, whereas its influence on uniqueness becomes stronger. These findings show that recommender systems adapt to user disengagement by reprioritizing content, highlighting algorithmic curation as a socio-technical process that shapes attention amid selective news exposure.

latest_articles.title: Black Lives Matter on the Ballot, in the Press: An Argument for Reporting the Long View of Contentious Solutions in Local Journalism
latest_articles.abstract: This paper investigates how local journalists in Austin, Texas reported on a 2021 ballot initiative mandating increased police staffing. Representing a backlash to 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, the initiative followed efforts to reallocate funds away from the Austin Police Department. Grounded in interviews with journalists who described their news choices and positionality in relation to the initiative, this case study reveals how contentious solutions to intractable social problems exacerbate tensions inherent to dominant journalistic norms. Journalists adhering to impartiality described the initiative’s underlying conflict narrowly to avoid the appearance of bias; more alarmingly, some acted as unfiltered conduits for false information by viewing coverage as a public forum for debate. We evaluate these findings against solutions-oriented journalism—an umbrella term for emerging paradigms that prioritize constructive reporting on solutions to engage news audiences in civic life—and demonstrate how these models fall short when solutions themselves are sites of intense social struggle. Inspired by journalists who resisted norms of impartiality and balance to investigate histories and trajectories of local social action, we encourage proponents of solutions-oriented journalism to prioritize rigorous, factual reporting of the long view for audiences to engage with solutions as people continuously struggle to enact them.

latest_articles.title: Soft Power from the Outside, Career Choice from the Inside: Understanding Job Attractions of Chinese Media Expats in Thailand
latest_articles.abstract: China’s global media expansion is often interpreted as a state-led soft power strategy. Yet little is known about how individual journalists enact this expansion while working overseas for Chinese media organizations. Taking Thailand as an empirical case, this article examines how Chinese journalists assigned to overseas postings come to view their roles as a worthwhile career decision. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Thailand and in-depth interviews with Chinese expat journalists, it argues that alignment with state goals emerges not from ideological commitment, but from personal motivations, career timing, and everyday practical reasoning. The article draws on Bourdieu’s concept of illusio to conceptualize this process as a socially grounded belief that the pursuit is worth investment. Journalists accept overseas postings insofar as these roles make sense within their own trajectories, at once professionally viable and personally meaningful. The findings complement state-centric models of media expansion and offers a framework for understanding journalists’ on-the-ground motivations amid broader transformations in global journalism.

latest_articles.title: The Many Notions of Audience Engagement: A Scoping Review
latest_articles.abstract: In recent years, “audience engagement” and “engaged journalism” have emerged as buzzwords in journalism studies. Audience engagement is regularly discussed as a potential remedy for declining trust in journalism and its precarious financial situation. Over the past two decades, journalism studies have thus extensively analyzed the concept, resulting in a vast body of literature on engagement. However, this has created definitional confusion around audience engagement, with numerous definitions, interpretations and characteristics of the concept discussed in existing scholarship. By conducting a systematic scoping review of 174 peer-reviewed journal articles on audience engagement, this study sheds closer light on the existing research on engagement, offers an overview on theoretical and empirical conceptualizations, and examines goals and challenges associated with engagement. The review highlights how audience engagement is examined and conceptualized in journalism scholarship, and identifies key directions for future research.

latest_articles.title: Immersion Matters: Virtual Reality Influences Personal and Systemic Bias Outcomes
latest_articles.abstract: Social psychological research has used traditional empathy-inducing strategies (e.g. reading, listening to, or watching narratives) to heighten recognition of and motivation to combat personal and systemic bias. We investigated whether a non-embodied 360° virtual reality (VR) experience increased recognition of and motivation to combat both personal and systemic racial bias and examined empathy as an underlying mechanism. Non-Black undergraduates in the United States (N = 313) were randomly assigned to (a) a non-embodied immersive 360° VR experience depicting racial discrimination, (b) an audio-only version of the same experience, or (c) a race-unrelated audio (control). VR exposure (vs. audio-only and control) heightened recognition of systemic bias, motivation to combat both systemic and personal bias, and perceptions of racism in isolated incidents. Emotional empathy, but not cognitive empathy, was a significant mediator. In contrast, the audio-only condition did not differ from the VR or control condition on personal and systemic bias outcomes or recognition of racism. These findings highlight the theoretical and practical value of non-embodied 360° immersive VR as a tool for combating personal and systemic bias.

latest_articles.title: African Community Media, AI, and the Question of Community Participation in the Disruptive Era
latest_articles.abstract: In this article, we examine the nexus of Southern African community newspapers’ sceptical AI integration and grassroots democracy. The sceptical approach to AI integration in marginalised media markets of Southern African community newspapers’ news ecosystems is interrogated. We respond to the questions: In what ways is the integration of AI tools in everyday news production routines within Southern African community media institutions defined by scepticism? What is the basis of scepticism amongst Southern African community media journalists? What are the implications for grassroots democracy in these communities? The Southern African community media under study are drawn from South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Namibia. Data were collected through in-depth semi-structured interviews with purposively sampled journalists and editors from these newsrooms. Findings show that the sceptical approach to AI adoption among Southern African community newspapers is largely driven by fears and concerns about AI’s documented mass production of misinformation and disinformation. In addition, the sceptical approach to AI adoption in these newsrooms is rooted in a lack of technical proficiency with AI tools and financial limitations occasioned by the decline in philanthropic funding.

latest_articles.title: Navigating Online Visibility: Construction of Feminine Identity in Chinese Influencers’ Affective Networked Publics
latest_articles.abstract: The rise of fashion and beauty influencers in China has produced highly visible representations of idealised femininity that increasingly appeal to young women and girls. This study examines how influencers on the Chinese social media platform Weibo discursively construct feminine identity through digital self-branding and how young women interpret and negotiate this mediated feminine visibility. By employing in-depth interviews with 31 Chinese urban young women and a feminist critical discourse analysis of 48 selected posts produced by leading female influencers, this study identifies three interrelated discursive resources through which idealised femininity is assembled: ambiguous feminism, an entrepreneurial beauty discourse, and aspirational consumption. Drawing on Berlant’s concept of intimate publics, the study argues that these discourses circulate affectively through relatability, producing both belonging and discipline within the community. Participants actively negotiate these representations through tactically extracting symbolic values and managing pressures to construct a legible feminine subjectivity. Furthermore, this study argues that asymmetric gendered power relations are reproduced through affective circulation within feminised digital spaces.

latest_articles.title: The Promise and Practice of Sharing Qualitative Data in Communication Research: Insights from the Qualitative Data Repository
latest_articles.abstract: As open science ideas gain traction in communication and media studies, qualitative researchers face unique challenges and opportunities in adopting transparent and reproducible practices. This article contributes to the growing conversation on open research infrastructures by introducing the Qualitative Data Repository (QDR) as a domain-specific solution for qualitative and multi-method data sharing. QDR is particularly well-equipped to manage data derived from human participants or existing media materials, both of which are widely used in this field. We explore how QDR’s infrastructure, services, and ethical frameworks can be adapted to the needs of communication scholars. First, we briefly outline the benefits of qualitative data sharing—including increased transparency, methodological rigor, and pedagogical value—while acknowledging possible barriers such as ethical concerns, time constraints, and disciplinary histories. We then review practical developments that have taken place over the last five years by scholars practicing some of the principles for trustworthy qualitative communication research laid out by Humphreys et al. (2021). Using examples from a wide variety of projects where QDR has already facilitated data publication and annotations for transparent inquiry, we illustrate how similar practices can be adopted systematically in communication research. We also highlight QDR’s support for researchers throughout the data lifecycle, from planning and consent to curation and controlled access. This article aims to demystify qualitative data sharing and encourage broader adoption among communication and media studies scholars by showcasing QDR’s model and its alignment with findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable principles. We argue that embracing more open and transparent research practices not only enhances the quality and visibility of individual projects but also fosters a more inclusive and collaborative scholarly community.

latest_articles.title: When Populism? Consistent and Opportunistic Populist Communication in the 2022 Brazilian Presidential Elections
latest_articles.abstract: When do presidential candidates use populist communication, and does its prevalence vary across policy domains? We address these questions using an original dataset of 11,885 tweets from nine Brazilian presidential candidates during the 2022 elections. Drawing on the ideational approach, we operationalize populist discourse as the co-occurrence of people-centrism and anti-elitism, measured with fine-tuned BERT-based classifiers, and classify policy domains with the Comparative Agendas Project framework. Our findings reveal substantial heterogeneity across candidates, challenging expectations that populist communication uniformly intensifies during campaigns or systematically varies across policy domains according to ideology. Rather than increasing uniformly during the campaign, populist appeals escalate strategically for some candidates as elections approach, while remaining stable for others throughout the electoral year. We propose a typology distinguishing opportunistic from consistent populists. Across policy domains, government operations serve as a baseline facilitating populist framing. Left-wing candidates increase populist rhetoric in labor/employment, consistent with issue ownership expectations, but right-wing candidates reduce populist appeals in their traditionally owned domains of law and crime and civil rights, contrary to expectations. Overall, we show that populism is neither a universal campaign imperative nor a content-neutral communication style, but a flexible discursive frame shaped by candidate strategy, electoral context, and policy content.

latest_articles.title: Observer v Actor: Exploring Individual Dispositions and Social Identity Influences on Incivility Perceptions and Performance
latest_articles.abstract: Sensitized by the expectancy violations theory (EVT) for the observer perspective and the social identity theory (SIT) for the actor position, the study surveyed 263 young, educated Nigerians to investigate whether personality traits shape perceptions of incivility, compared to whether social identities, especially partisanship and ethnicity, provided an explanation of reported participation in uncivil political discourse on social media. Using correlations, hierarchical regression models, and moderation analyses, support was found for both assumptions, with agreeableness significantly predicting perceived incivility, and partisanship explaining self-reported incivility; however, the study also found that personality traits, especially agreeableness and conscientiousness, served a regulating function on social identity’s influence on uncivil discursive behavior. The implications of these findings for incivility research, including the lack of support for ethnicity’s influence on behavior, are discussed.

latest_articles.title: Narratives of Embodied Knowledge: Toward Reciprocal Participation in Public Dialogue
latest_articles.abstract: Public dialogue forums convene community members to discuss the impact and possibilities of topics of civic importance. Their credibility often depends on the participation of historically underrepresented groups whose lived experiences are central to the issues discussed. Using the lens of embodied knowledge, an informant narrates his experience with public dialogues on policing. The narratives demonstrate forums served as constitutive of 1) paradox, 2) reciprocity, 3) contestation of hegemonic “common sense,” and 4) connection to an influential community position on the police hiring committee. The findings advance concepts toward an ethically responsible framework of reciprocal participation in public dialogue.

latest_articles.title: The role of democratic values in shaping perceptions of political incivility in European liberal democracies
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates whether citizens’ perceptions of political incivility converge across liberal democracies and the extent to which individual orientations towards democracy and democratic values are associated with sensitivity to incivility. Drawing on a comparative survey conducted in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom ( N = 3500), it examines the individual factors associated with sensitivity to incivility. The results show that support for democracy and endorsement of democratic values are the most influential predictors of sensitivity to incivility, with higher levels associated with greater sensitivity, whereas anti-political attitudes are associated with lower sensitivity. These findings indicate that sensitivity to incivility is primarily associated with citizens’ orientations towards democracy and its normative principles rather than with national contextual differences. Citizens in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom assess incivility in remarkably similar ways, despite differences in electoral systems, media systems, and political cultures.
affiliations: Department of Communication and Social Research, ‘Sapienza’ University of Rome, Italy

latest_articles.title: Safe havens for hate: the challenge of moderating online extremism

latest_articles.title: Balancing Originality and Strategy: The 4A Modes Framework of Human-AI Collaboration in Advertising Creativity
latest_articles.abstract: Balancing creative originality with strategic discipline remains a fundamental paradox in advertising creativity. Although generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can produce novel recombinations of creative elements, it may not reliably align with brand strategy and campaign-specific executional requirements. To address this tension, organizations are reconfiguring creative workflows through new forms of human-AI collaboration. Drawing on an inductive multi-case study of five advertising organizations, including an incumbent agency and an AI-native startup, this study develops the 4A Modes Framework of Human-AI Collaboration. Organized along two dimensions of AI autonomy and process embeddedness, this framework identifies four modes of collaboration: Augmentation, Automation, Agentic, and Alliance. Furthermore, we identify two evolutionary paths through which organizations systematically navigate this tension: Process Integration and Native Innovation. Across both paths, micro-ambidexterity enables practitioners and teams to flexibly switch between and recombine collaboration modes within a single production process. Overall, these findings provide a theoretical lens for understanding the structural transformation of creative production and offer practical guidance for achieving effective and sustainable human-AI symbiosis.

latest_articles.title: Journalistic Routines and the Social Construction of Race: A Critical Discourse Analysis of the Tyreek Hill Police Encounter
latest_articles.abstract: To gauge U.S. journalism’s post-2020 racial reckoning, this article examines news coverage of football player Tyreek Hill’s police encounter in September 2024. Using Critical Discourse Analysis to interpret and explain digital media texts, this project mimics the contingency of the internet and considers local, national, legacy, digital-only, and sports outlets. Overall, it finds that news discourse continues to operate through a white racial frame. Even outlets that acknowledged systemic inequities or foregrounded the perspectives of the racially marginalized could recreate this dominant perspective, reinforcing tropes such as Black criminality, victim blaming, and deference to official sources. It’s thus argued that routine journalistic practices such as descriptive reporting, bothsidesism, headline conventions, reliance on official sources, and other supposedly objective norms, actually limit social discourse and the ability to have honest, good faith conversations about race. The project further highlights coverage that did counter the white racial frame and ultimately argues such coverage should be the standard. These practices are more ethical (i.e., take responsibility for the social consequences of news narratives) and provide a more nuanced and rigorous approximation of truth.

latest_articles.title: Journalism as Science’s Watchdog: The Vibrancy and Vulnerability of an Increasingly Diverse Ecosystem
latest_articles.abstract: Watchdog science journalism, broadly understood, investigates, exposes, and warns society of the misuses and abuses of science methods, processes, outcomes, and authority by those practicing, funding, and/or using science in the public domain. Amid rising threats to research integrity, this thematic issue provides a first comprehensive set of empirical and conceptual insights into how this type of journalism is becoming both vibrant and vulnerable. It reveals that watchdog science journalism is recognized as essential by members of the public and by journalists alike and is empowered by an increasingly diverse set of actors, both within and beyond traditional journalism. Yet, ongoing challenges within and beyond the news industry are putting pressure on this role, undermining journalists’ capacity to effectively scrutinize and sound the alarm about research integrity problems that put the public interest at risk.

latest_articles.title: Watchdog Science Journalism: How Retraction Watch Fosters Accountability in Science
latest_articles.abstract: Although science reporters have long been urged to adopt the role of the journalistic watchdog, scholars have not extensively examined how this role can be understood conceptually or in practice. This exploratory case study examines Retraction Watch, founded in 2010, as an illuminating example of watchdog science journalism that holds science to account around the epistemological claim, central to science’s cultural authority, that it is self-correcting. Drawing on a thematic analysis of interviews with senior staff at the site and scholars who study retractions, the study finds that the site has undertaken accountability journalism of the little-scrutinised phenomenon of retractions, has reported systematically on retractions, has questioned and determined the reasons for retractions, has created a database of retractions to aid science in its self-correction, and has provided knowledge-based journalism for its specialist public interested in scientific integrity. The article argues that Retraction Watch has expanded beyond journalism to operate as a novel journalistic hybrid institution that combines science journalism with the scientific infrastructure of its database, activities underpinned by a normative value of accountability. As a journalistic hybrid institution, it illustrates what future organisational forms of science journalism might look like.

latest_articles.title: Branding the invisible: Big Tech, naming submarine cables, and the politics of infrastructure (in)visibility
latest_articles.abstract: Submarine cables have historically been invisible: buried, technical and obscured by conventions such as security and language including naming practises that prioritised function over storytelling. However, as Big Tech companies like Google have emerged as major cable investors, increasingly shifting from consortium to sole or private ownership, they have disrupted the cable industry in many ways. This paper demonstrates this disruption through the naming practises adopted by Google for its privately-owned cables. It argues that names are not neutral descriptors but tools that selectively make infrastructure visible and culturally significant which transforms cables from technical objects to cultural products. This allows for cables to be branded and marketed – in the case of Google, as part of a unified brand story. Through storytelling potentials embedded within names (including gender, inclusion, indigenous references), Google signals its progressive credentials and tells a story that connects its different product and services. Thus, nomenclature allows for the company to imbue infrastructure with values while obscuring risks and impact of Google’s cable ownership. Drawing on postcolonial perspectives, infrastructure studies, marketing communication, and political economy of communication, this paper examines how language shapes perception of submarine cables including its ownership, control, risks, power, and public relations.

latest_articles.title: Contributions and future directions in African sports media scholarship: a scoping review
latest_articles.abstract: A scoping review of research on sport media in and about the African continent was conducted to examine the trends related to the geography of knowledge, sport context, and theoretical and methodological frameworks. This review examined 174 articles that were published in 86 outlets. The analysis revealed the influence of South African regional hegemony, with authors from South African institutions producing the most articles, and the geographic context of South Africa was also the most investigated within the sample. In addition, there was a significant colonial influence in the sport context, with sports like football and rugby amongst the most examined. This colonial lens also influenced the theoretical contributions, with Western frameworks more often utilized compared with African theories and concepts. Directions for future research based on the results of the scoping review are discussed.
affiliations: University of Maryland, College Park, U.S.A.

latest_articles.title: Verifying Out of Alarm, or Alarmed After Verification? A Three-Wave Cross-Lagged Analysis of Multidimensional Risk Perceptions and Verification Behavior Amid Climate Misinformation in China
latest_articles.abstract: Risk communication research often assumes that heightened risk perception drives subsequent behavioral responses, yet this perception-to-behavior logic remains underexamined. This study differentiates personal-level and societal-level risk perception and investigates their reciprocal associations with verification behavior in the context of climate change misinformation. Using three-wave panel data from China and cross-lagged structural equation modeling, results reveal a clear asymmetry: neither type of risk perception predicted subsequent verification. Instead, verification consistently increased societal risk perception over time, but not personal-level risk perception. These findings challenge the linear perception-to-behavior assumption and highlight a behavior-to-perception feedback pathway.
affiliations: Hong Kong Baptist University, Kowloon, Hong Kong

latest_articles.title: Aramco Television: Articulations of Social Identity in Television Adaptation 1957–1970
latest_articles.abstract: In the postcolonial era, the Joint Arabian American Company (ARAMCO) established the first television channel in the Arabian Gulf region, Aramco Television. Local audiences initially resisted the medium, perceiving television as a colonial instrument. Drawing on archival documents and interviews with experts and media producers associated with the channel, this article examines how Aramco Television adapted both the television device and its content to local Gulf contexts. It argues that this process relied on cultural foundations and selective filtering strategies to make the medium socially and culturally acceptable. The findings suggest that adaptation was not simply a matter of transferring foreign media forms, but a process of negotiation through which imported technologies and content were localized, appropriated, and made culturally meaningful. Aramco Television represented an early example of Gulf media adaptation in which foreign media forms contributed to emerging articulations of regional identity.

latest_articles.title: Skin Tone as a Visual Cue in Political Campaigns: Evidence from Elections in Mexico
latest_articles.abstract: Research has long established that physical appearance and phenotypical traits influence how people evaluate political candidates. Skin color is one of the visual cues the electorate perceives during campaigns and media coverage, and a possible source of prejudice and bias. Here we use computational visual analysis to investigate the association between skin tone and electoral success during the 2024 Mexican Federal Elections. Our analyses incorporate important correlates not considered in prior research, most prominently news coverage, political ads, and social media use. We also account for geographic differences in average skin tone, explicitly modeling a source of variation that is obscured when skin tone is analyzed disregarding contextual baselines. We use fixed effects generalized linear models to control for state and party variation as well as candidate-level demographics, political experience, incumbency status, and media presence (news coverage, political ads, and social media use). Consistent with past work, we find that as candidates’ skin tone becomes darker, their predicted vote share declines. However, news coverage, political ads, and social media use are, together, more important predictors of electoral success than skin tone, indicating that this phenotypical trait is not as prominent a visual cue as earlier research suggested.
affiliations: Annenberg School for Communication, University of Pennsylvania, USA

latest_articles.title: From Hate Speech to Collective Action Intentions: The Role of Counter-Speech and Accuracy Cues Among Targeted Minorities
latest_articles.abstract: Online hate speech targeting minority groups poses a significant social identity threat to those affected, often prompting coping strategies like out-group avoidance or derogation, which can harm intergroup relations in diverse societies. However, collective action as an empowering response has received limited attention in this context. Drawing on the social identity model of collective action (SIMCA), this study examines both the mechanisms and boundary conditions of online hate speech’s impact on minority groups. Across two experiments ( N Study1 = 328 Muslims; N Study2 = 583 Latinos), we find that online hate speech increases group-based injustice, which in turn drives collective action intentions, supporting the SIMCA. This effect is amplified when information embedded in the online hate speech is perceived as inaccurate or flagged for inaccuracy. In Study 2, we further demonstrate that counter-speech can reduce group-based injustice and, when paired with low-accuracy hate speech, enhance collective efficacy beliefs.
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles, USA
University of California, Santa Barbara, USA

latest_articles.title: Driving and Drivering
latest_articles.abstract: Autonomous mobility does not invent distributed perception; it reorganises older relations among eye, body, vehicle and street into a predictive media infrastructure. Focussing on sensorised urban environments, this article theorises the post-ocular sensorium as a formation in which cameras, lidar, radar, V2X systems, digital twins and fleet memories convert the street into classifications, probabilities, alerts and trajectories. Through the cases of smart intersections, Chattanooga’s MLK Smart Corridor, autonomous-vehicle misclassification, routing anomalies and infrastructural error, the article examines how perception migrates from the driver’s eye to a lattice of vehicles, roadside instruments, municipal platforms and proprietary protocols. It argues that this migration produces not only new capacities for safety and anticipation, but also new forms of infrastructural illusion, in which model, map, message or feed slips out of register with the street it governs. The Chattanooga case is used to show that smart corridors are never merely technical prototypes: they inherit longer histories of urban planning, racialised displacement, pedestrian vulnerability and civic repair. The article therefore proposes Drivering as an ethics of acknowledgement for infrastructural seeing. Drivering names the civic discipline of making distributed road perception technically inspectable, publicly contestable, historically situated and ethically unfinished. Its conclusion is not a nostalgic recovery of human control, nor a refusal of machine perception, but a demand that networked sight remain answerable to the lives it classifies, anticipates and moves.

latest_articles.title: Platform infrastructures of reading: Postliterary Attention Theory and summary-first interfaces
latest_articles.abstract: Contemporary discourse frequently diagnoses an “attention crisis,” framing distraction and overload as individual or psychological failures. This article argues that the crisis is better understood as a transformation in the media-technological conditions of reading. It develops Postliterary Attention Theory (PLAT) to explain how platform infrastructures organise textual encounter through three mechanisms: pre-legibility, in which ranking and summary layers shape salience before reading; labour shift, in which platforms compress and pre-frame texts while readers inherit burdens of verification and contextual reconstruction; and temporal governance, in which refresh rhythms, notifications, and metric feedback normalise fragmented engagement. The outcome is stratified durational literacy: unequal capacity for sustained reading, interpretive depth, and visibility across different infrastructural and socioeconomic conditions. The article advances three propositions—attention as embodied media labour, algorithmic co-reading as hybrid literacy, and fragmentation as structural affect—and offers a conceptual demonstration of how PLAT may be operationalised through threshold analysis, with summary-first interfaces and AI-generated overviews treated as exemplary reading thresholds in discovery environments. It concludes by reframing media power as the organisation of literacy and by outlining a comparative agenda for studying reading under convergent media conditions.

latest_articles.title: Romance changes everything: player engagement with romantic video game content
latest_articles.abstract: This study investigates the diverse ways that players engage with romantic video game content, addressing a gap in existing player typologies. Drawing on hundreds of hours of gameplay and a decade of online community observation, we extend research on player classification by highlighting a spectrum of romantic player types shaped by distinct motivations, interests, and behaviors. The analysis reveals that romantic engagement is not monolithic. Players can interact with romance emotionally, strategically, incidentally, and spectatorially. External materials, such as guides, mods, and fan-created works, play a significant role in shaping these experiences. By situating romantic gameplay within broader paratextual and community contexts, we demonstrate that romance in games serves multiple functions, from emotional exploration to achievement and narrative support. The findings highlight the need for game designers to consider the complexity of romantic engagement, informing future design and research in video games and interactive media.
affiliations: Herberger Institute for Design and the Arts, Arizona State University

latest_articles.title: AI-Mediated Mental Health Support: The Role of Attachment Orientation and Psychological Distress
latest_articles.abstract: General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are increasingly serving as quasi-social agents, representing a novel form of informal AI-mediated help-seeking. This study examined associations between adult attachment orientations (Experiences in Close Relationships-Relationship Structures questionnaire), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales–21), and the use of GenAI for mental health support. In a nonprobability sample of 584 Israeli adult GenAI users, 29.3 percent reported having turned to these models at least once for emotional support, coping advice, or mental health assistance; the proportion reached 47.0 percent among those reporting severe distress. These self-reported figures reflect any such contact, from a single exchange to sustained use. Hierarchical logistic regression identified distress as the strongest psychological correlate of use. Younger age and female gender predicted use. Attachment anxiety was associated with use, but this association did not remain significant once distress was included, a pattern consistent with the shared variance between the two constructs. Attachment avoidance was negatively but nonsignificantly associated with use. Findings position general-purpose GenAI as an accessible, low-barrier resource disproportionately used by distressed individuals. The high uptake among severely distressed users (47.0 percent) points to potential safety concerns and to a need for systematic evaluation of the safety, crisis-response quality, and clinical-displacement risks of consumer-facing AI use.

latest_articles.title: Internet Addiction Disorder and Cybersecurity Risk: A Neurobiological and Behavioral Review
latest_articles.abstract: Internet addiction disorder (IAD) has attracted substantial clinical and scientific interest over the past two decades. Although the condition remains outside formal diagnostic frameworks in the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, accumulating neuroimaging evidence demonstrates that compulsive Internet use is associated with disruptions in dopaminergic reward circuitry and prefrontal cortical function that closely parallel those observed in substance use disorders. These neurobiological changes, encompassing impaired executive function, elevated impulsivity, and heightened reward sensitivity, may carry implications for cybersecurity. Available evidence suggests that individuals exhibiting addictive patterns of Internet use show reduced compliance with security protocols, increased vulnerability to social engineering, and elevated engagement in risky online behaviors, although directionality cannot be established with confidence given the predominantly cross-sectional evidence base. The present narrative review synthesizes evidence from addiction neuroscience, clinical psychology, and cybersecurity research to propose a mechanistic account of the IAD–cybersecurity risk relationship. The review identifies impaired prefrontal inhibitory control as the central neurobiological mediator linking IAD to cybersecurity vulnerability, mediated primarily through impulsivity and compounded by the attentional and affective characteristics that render addicted individuals susceptible to social engineering. Drawing on literature spanning 2017–2026, the review also situates this account within a contemporary regulatory context, including the documented acceleration of problematic Internet use during the COVID-19 pandemic, Australia’s landmark social media minimum age legislation, and an influential 2026 civil verdict in which a U.S. jury found major platform operators liable for harms arising from addictive design. Clinical, organizational, and policy implications are discussed.
affiliations: Queen’s Medical Centre, Nottingham, United Kingdom.

latest_articles.title: Parent–Child Play and Media Addiction in Adolescence: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study
latest_articles.abstract: Although media addiction is a recognized public health concern, the theoretical framework surrounding its longitudinal development remains relatively underdeveloped. This study addresses that gap by evaluating a developmental model that traces a path from early parent–child play at age 6 to adolescent media addiction at age 14, with executive function and peer attachment at age 10 examined as parallel mediators. We used three waves of data from a representative sample of 1,130 parent–child dyads in the Panel Study on Korean Children. Early parent–child play at age 6 significantly predicted higher executive function at age 10, which subsequently predicted lower media addiction at age 14. This indirect path via executive function was statistically significant. Conversely, the indirect effect through peer attachment was not significant, as peer attachment was unrelated to both early play and subsequent media addiction. The direct effect of parent–child play on adolescent media addiction was nonsignificant, demonstrating that the protective influence of early family play operates through cognitive mechanisms rather than social bonds. These findings shift the clinical focus from proximal adolescent factors to early prevention, emphasizing middle childhood as a critical therapeutic window for bolstering executive function to mitigate later media addiction risks.
affiliations: School of Business Administration, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, South Korea.
Department of Early Childhood Education, Kyungnam University, Changwon, South Korea.
